This owner starts very high but concedes steadily once talks stay open — your very low opening and cautious 30% gap moves with an open, cooperative argument won almost all the way; keep the same low open, the 0.3 concession fraction, and an open tone/stability argument.

This owner concedes steadily toward a stabilisation outcome and stops once the price nears the midpoint of initial quotes; keep the relatively firm opening and small, steady concession steps (≈30%), lead with a cooperative stability argument and maintain an open, non‑adversarial tone.

With a supplier showing spare capacity who concedes early then hits a firm floor, keep a low opening, move faster (take a larger fraction of the gap each round) to lock in early concessions, and lead with leverage-oriented arguments in a collaborative tone.

This supplier concedes steadily but then plateaus and only gives the final small fall after persistent pressure; for the next RFQ open a bit lower and close faster (increase your gap-step to ~40–50%), lead with a competitive/market-pressure argument first, and keep a confident but cooperative tone.

This spare-capacity supplier concedes steadily but halts quickly once prices near your level; keep an open tone and a similarly low opening but move a larger share of the gap per round and lead with a leverage argument to capture more value faster.

Keep the same firm tone and low opening, but move faster—take a larger fraction of the gap each round because this supplier cuts quickly early and then stalls, so slowing your pace leaves value on the table.

This supplier concedes a lot early when capacity is available but plateaus near ~0.80 — keep an open tone, open a bit lower to capture more room, and take larger early steps (close more of the gap in the first rounds) to force the deeper concessions before they stop.

This family-owned supplier makes small early concessions then freezes price—respond by opening lower and keep steady modest gap-closings (~30% per round), but switch to an open-book/collaborative argument and softer tone to exploit spare capacity.

This owner-type holds near its first offer and only trims tiny amounts late—open lower than before and concede in smaller steps, lead with the approval/constraints argument and keep a firm tone to extract more value.

They made one small concession then stayed at a frozen group price—your low opener plus steady 30% gap moves and a firm tone won near-optimal terms; keep that opening and concession pace for similar renewals and avoid pushing after their single drop.

With family-owned, routine bundling suppliers who have spare capacity and low approval thresholds, your current low opening and steady 30% concession pace worked well—keep that opening, the same fraction, an open friendly tone, and lead with the bundling/volume argument first.

This owner group concedes a little early then plateaus when capacity/approval limits bite, so open lower to leave more room and then concede more slowly (smaller share each round); lead with the supply‑security/long‑term partnership argument and keep the firm tone.

This group supplier concedes significantly early but then stalls around a mid-range; open a bit lower and close more of the gap each round (increase the fraction) to capture those early concessions, while keeping the open tone and leading with a market-benchmark/cost-comparison argument.

With a founder-run supplier who is cash-sensitive and facing spare capacity, an aggressive low opening plus measured 30% gap moves work — they will concede under RFQ pressure and stop once they hit your opening. Keep the low opening but push harder earlier — increase the per‑round share moved (e.g. from 30% to ~50%) so you extract concessions before this private, quality‑focused owner plateaus; lead with a quality‑first argument and stay open in tone.

Keep the high opening close to the supplier’s level and maintain the conservative (30%) step size — it secured near-optimal terms here. Start with a stabilisation/framing argument in an open tone and keep patience; repeat this approach for similar single-bidder, stability-seeking owners.
This supplier matches a high, firm opening quickly to reach stability; keep opening near your target, concede only a small fraction each round, and lead with the stabilization argument.

This supplier gives one early concession then plateaus near a clear floor; open a bit lower and move a larger share of the gap faster, lead with the RFQ/competitive leverage argument, and keep the firm tone.

Supplier with spare capacity makes a big early cut then freezes at a firm floor; keep a low opening and firm tone, lead with leverage/volume arguments, but move a larger share of the gap each round (e.g. ~50%) to capture more value before they stop conceding.

This supplier concedes quickly from an initial high but plateaus near the mid-0.9s, so keep the same trade package (short payment terms and multi‑month contract), open with the stabilisation argument and stay cooperative — the same tone and moves produced an almost optimal outcome.

Keep the firm, steady hold strategy and lead with the stability/long‑term contract argument while offering payment_days=30 and extended contract months early — this supplier concedes quickly from an initial high but stops once stability is secured, so don’t soften pace or change tone.

This supplier concedes steadily but stops around a clear floor (~0.80); keep the same small, measured price steps and continue offering payment/lead-time trades early, but add one extra concessionable term (e.g., a short volume commitment) to pull the final few ticks.

This family-run renewal supplier made one small concession, then held firm, so expect little movement after its first adjustment. With a strong result, keep the term-for-price trade, but make any price movement conditional rather than continuing to raise your offer.

This routine-focused family supplier conceded in progressively smaller steps, so expect room to narrow as talks progress. Keep a reciprocal long-term bundling trade, and lead with practical value from using its spare capacity rather than adding one-way commitments.
